claim: Dyslexia is a prevalent reading disability whose underlying mechanisms are still disputed.
source: Dyslexia is a prevalent reading disability whose underlying mechanisms are still disputed.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Dyslexics showed a faster decay of implicit memory effects on both behavioral and ERP measures, with similar time constants.
source: Dyslexics showed a faster decay of implicit memory effects on both measures, with similar time constants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing dyslexics and controls.

claim: Faster decay of implicit memory also characterized the impact of sound regularities in benefitting dyslexics' oral reading rate.
source: Finally, faster decay of implicit memory also characterized the impact of sound regularities in benefitting dyslexics' oral reading rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the reading task in the study.

claim: Dyslexics' benefit from repetition decreased faster as a function of the time interval from the previous reading of the same non-word.
source: Their benefit decreased faster as a function of the time interval from the previous reading of the same non-word.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics' shorter neural adaptation paradoxically accounts for their longer reading times.
source: We propose that dyslexics' shorter neural adaptation paradoxically accounts for their longer reading times, since it reduces their temporal window of integration of past stimuli, resulting in noisier and less reliable predictions for both simple and complex stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Shorter neural adaptation reduces dyslexics' temporal window of integration of past stimuli, resulting in noisier and less reliable predictions.
source: since it reduces their temporal window of integration of past stimuli, resulting in noisier and less reliable predictions for both simple and complex stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and theoretical framework.

claim: Less reliable predictions limit dyslexics' acquisition of reading expertise.
source: Less reliable predictions limit their acquisition of reading expertise.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the long-term consequences of the observed deficit.

claim: Dyslexics consistently show difficulties in some language-related skills such as verbal working memory.
source: Their general reasoning skills are within the normal range (or above), but they consistently show difficulties in some language-related skills such as verbal working memory (e.g. Torgeson and Goldman, 1977) and phonological manipulations (which typically also load on short-term memory [e.g. Landerl et al., 1997]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dyslexics consistently show difficulties in phonological manipulations.
source: Their general reasoning skills are within the normal range (or above), but they consistently show difficulties in some language-related skills such as verbal working memory (e.g. Torgeson and Goldman, 1977) and phonological manipulations (which typically also load on short-term memory [e.g. Landerl et al., 1997]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dyslexics often have higher thresholds in simple perceptual discrimination tasks.
source: Dyslexics also often have higher thresholds in simple perceptual discrimination tasks (Mcanally and Stein, 1996; Witton et al., 1998; Hämäläinen et al., 2013), particularly when administered with serial presentations (Ben-Yehudah and Ahissar, 2004; discussed in Ramus and Ahissar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dyslexics' higher thresholds in perceptual discrimination tasks are particularly evident when administered with serial presentations.
source: Dyslexics also often have higher thresholds in simple perceptual discrimination tasks (Mcanally and Stein, 1996; Witton et al., 1998; Hämäläinen et al., 2013), particularly when administered with serial presentations (Ben-Yehudah and Ahissar, 2004; discussed in Ramus and Ahissar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Listeners use a repeated reference tone as an 'anchor' in frequency discrimination tasks.
source: They assessed a well-documented observation (Harris, 1948) that listeners use a repeated reference tone as an 'anchor', and that their performance was improved in protocols that included this reference tone compared with a no-reference protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Listeners' performance is improved in protocols that include a repeated reference tone compared with a no-reference protocol.
source: They assessed a well-documented observation (Harris, 1948) that listeners use a repeated reference tone as an 'anchor', and that their performance was improved in protocols that included this reference tone compared with a no-reference protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The benefit that dyslexics obtained from repetition of a reference tone was smaller than that obtained by good readers.
source: The benefit that dyslexics obtained from this repetition was smaller than that obtained by 'good readers'.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Ahissar et al., 2006).

claim: A similar deficit was found in dyslexics' benefit from repetition of speech sounds.
source: A similar deficit was found in dyslexics' benefit from repetition of speech sounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from previous research mentioned in the context.

claim: Dyslexics have a deficit in using sound stimuli as perceptual anchors for the formation of sound predictions.
source: This led to the hypothesis that dyslexics have a deficit in using sound stimuli as perceptual anchors for the formation of sound predictions (Ahissar et al., 2006; Ahissar, 2007; Oganian and Ahissar, 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Listeners implicitly infer the mean frequency even when it is not presented explicitly.
source: This model assumes that listeners implicitly infer the mean (frequency) even when it is not presented explicitly.
evidence: This is based on a computational model from previous research (Raviv et al., 2012).

claim: The inferred mean of previous stimuli (prior) is combined with the representation of the current stimulus to form an integrated percept (posterior).
source: The inferred mean of previous stimuli (prior) is combined with the representation of the current stimulus, and forms an integrated percept (posterior).
evidence: This is based on a computational model from previous research.

claim: The resulting percept is contracted (biased) towards the mean frequency.
source: The resulting percept is contracted (biased) towards that mean (the 'contraction bias'; Woodrow, 1933; Preuschhof et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the general population, 'noisier' listeners weigh the prior more than 'less noisy' listeners when integrating the prior with current representation.
source: Indeed, in the general population, 'noisier' listeners weigh the prior more than 'less noisy' listeners when integrating the prior with current representation, resulting in their larger contraction bias.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Dyslexics' bias is smaller than controls' even though they tend to be 'noisier' listeners.
source: Jaffe-Dax et al. (2015) found that dyslexics' bias is smaller than controls' even though they tend to be 'noisier' listeners.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The representation of the first tone is contracted towards the prior more than the second tone because of noise added during encoding and retention in memory.
source: In the two-tone frequency discrimination task, the representation of the first tone is contracted towards the prior more than the second tone, because of the noise added to its representation during the encoding and retention in memory through the inter-stimulus time interval.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational model and task design.

claim: The contraction of the first tone towards the prior can increase the perceived difference between the two tones in the trial and improve discrimination (Bias+ trials).
source: The contraction of the first tone towards the prior can increase the perceived difference between the two tones in the trial, and hence improve discrimination (Bias+ trials; e.g., trial t in Figure 1A)
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The contraction of the first tone towards the prior could decrease the perceived difference between the two tones and disrupt performance (Bias- trials).
source: alternatively, it could decrease the perceived difference between the two tones and disrupt performance (Bias-; e.g., trial t−1 in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The difference in performance between Bias+ and Bias- trials reflects the magnitude of the contraction bias.
source: The difference in performance between Bias+ and Bias- trials reflects the magnitude of the contraction bias (i.e. context effect).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and model.

claim: Dyslexics' underweighting of the prior yields a smaller contraction bias.
source: Dyslexics' underweighting of the prior yields a smaller contraction bias, namely a smaller performance difference between these two types of trials (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The overall accuracy of the two groups in the frequency discrimination task did not differ.
source: The overall accuracy of the two groups in this task did not differ (controls' mean % correct ± SEM = 75.3 ± 1.6, dyslexics' = 73 ± 1.9; z = 1.3, n.s. Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Dyslexics' frequency difference predictor did not differ from controls'.
source: Dyslexics' frequency difference predictor did not differ from controls' (Figure 1C; z = 1.6, n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The impact of the context effect of the most recent trial was similar in the two groups.
source: The impact of the context effect of the most recent trial (ITI ≈ 1.5 s) was also similar in the two groups (z = 0.05, n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Dyslexics' bias towards the global mean was significantly smaller than controls'.
source: However, dyslexics' bias towards the global mean was significantly smaller than controls' (z = 2.7, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The difference in controls between the contributions of the Global and Recent contexts was larger than that found in dyslexics.
source: Indeed, the difference in controls between the contributions of the Global (all previous trials except the most recent one) and Recent contexts was larger than that found in dyslexics (z = 2.4, p<0.05. Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In both groups, the contribution of Recent context was significantly above zero.
source: Importantly, in both groups, the contribution of Recent context was significantly above zero (controls: z = 4.4, p<0.0001; dyslexics: z = 4.7, p<0.00001; Wilcoxon tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: For both groups, performance was better at longer ITIs.
source: For both groups, performance was better at longer ITIs (mean d' ± SEM for the four ITIs was 0.48 ± 0.05, 0.57 ± 0.05, 0.71 ± 0.06 and 0.78 ± 0.06, respectively; χ2=54.2, p<10−10. Friedman test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Controls' performance was slightly more accurate than dyslexics' performance across all ITIs.
source: Across all ITIs, controls' (n = 23) performance was slightly more accurate than dyslexics' performance (n = 25; mean d' ± SEM of controls = 0.71 ± 0.07, dyslexics = 0.56 ± 0.07; z = 2.0, p<0.05. Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: There was no significant interaction between group and ITI.
source: There was no significant interaction between group and ITI (group x ITI; F3,46 = 1.4, n.s. Repeated Measures ANOVA test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: The decay of contraction bias was significantly faster among dyslexics.
source: Evaluating the dynamics of the contraction bias as a function of ITI showed that its decay was significantly faster among dyslexics, as illustrated in Figure 2B (dashed line) and Figure 2C bottom (controls' τ = 6 ± 0.9 s, dyslexics' τ = 2.9 ± 0.8 s; mean ± SEM; z = 2.2, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The two other parameters (α and β) of the exponential decay model did not differ between the two groups for behavioral contraction bias.
source: The two other parameters did not differ between the two groups (α for controls = 0.7 ± 0.1 d', α for dyslexics = 0.5 ± 0.1 d'; z = 1, n.s.; β for controls = 2.3 ± 0.8 d', β for dyslexics = 4 ± 0.9 d'; z = 1.9, n.s. Mann-Whitney U tests)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: The neural mechanism that mediates the inference of the prior frequency is neural adaptation.
source: We hypothesized that the neural mechanism that mediates the inference of the prior frequency is neural adaptation, which is an automatic, stimulus-specific form of memory (Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous research cited.

claim: The time constant of context effects in sound discrimination is the same as that of cortical adaptation to sounds.
source: Importantly, it has been found that the time constant of context effects in sound discrimination is the same as that of cortical adaptation to sounds (Lu et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: N1 and P2 are the two prominent ERP components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex.
source: The two prominent ERP components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex are N1 and P2 (Sheehan et al., 2005; Mayhew et al., 2010), which peak at 100 and 200 ms from stimulus onset, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: N1 peaks at 100 ms from stimulus onset.
source: The two prominent ERP components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex are N1 and P2 (Sheehan et al., 2005; Mayhew et al., 2010), which peak at 100 and 200 ms from stimulus onset, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: P2 peaks at 200 ms from stimulus onset.
source: The two prominent ERP components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex are N1 and P2 (Sheehan et al., 2005; Mayhew et al., 2010), which peak at 100 and 200 ms from stimulus onset, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Only the magnitude of P2 showed sensitivity to the frequency prior in a previous study.
source: However, in our previous study, where we assessed sensitivity to the frequency prior (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015), only the magnitude of P2 showed such sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In both groups, the magnitude of the P2 responses was smallest in the block with the shortest ITI (1.5 s).
source: In both groups, the magnitude of the P2 responses was smallest in the block with the shortest ITI (1.5 s) when P2 adaptation was substantial, and increased (recovered) with longer ITIs, as adaptation gradually decayed (χ2 = 65.7, p<10−13. Friedman test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Among dyslexics, P2 reached its peak magnitude by 6 s ITI.
source: Among dyslexics, P2 reached its peak magnitude by 6 s ITI (Figure 2A, red dot-dashed line)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Controls' P2 was larger at 9 s ITIs than at 6 s ITIs.
source: whereas controls' P2 was larger at 9 s ITIs than at 6 s ITIs (Figure 2A, blue dotted line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The time constant of the recovery of P2 and the time constant of the behavioral context effect were similar.
source: As was evident when comparing the time constant of the recovery of P2 (time constant of its adaptation) and the time constant of the behavioral context effect, the two were similar, though P2 decay was slightly (but not significantly; z for controls = 0.2, n.s.; z for dyslexics = 0.5, n.s. Wilcoxon tests) slower than the behavioral time constant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Dyslexics' shorter adaptation was also found in the N1 ERP component.
source: Indeed, dyslexics' shorter adaptation was also found in this ERP component.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Dyslexics' N1 almost fully recovered at an ITI of 3 s, whereas the N1 at this ITI was still substantially adapted in controls.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3A and B, dyslexics' N1 almost fully recovered (regained full magnitude) at an ITI of 3 s, whereas the N1 at this ITI was still substantially 'adapted' in controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Only the rate of decay (τ) of N1 adaptation differed between the two groups.
source: Fitting the same exponential model, we found here too that only the rate of decay differed between the two groups (Figure 3C; τ for controls = 5.1 ± 0.8 s, τ for dyslexics = 1.3 ± 0.4 s; mean ± SEM; z = 4.2, p<0.0001. Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The two other estimated parameters (α and β) of N1 adaptation were similar between groups.
source: whereas the two other estimated parameters were similar (α for controls = −131 ± 20 μV x ms, α for dyslexics = −109 ± 16 μV x ms; z = 0.7, n.s.; β for controls = 497 ± 120 μV x ms, β for dyslexics = 750 ± 132 μV x ms; z = 1.1, n.s. Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Across groups, N1 adaptation was significantly shorter than that of P2.
source: Across groups, N1 adaptation was significantly shorter than that of P2 (z = 3.7, p<0.0005. Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: There was no interaction between group and ERP component (N1/P2) rate of decay of adaptation.
source: There was no interaction between group and ERP component (N1/P2) rate of decay of adaptation (z = 0.7, n.s. Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2a.

claim: Controls' P2 recovery was significantly slower than dyslexics' in the passive condition.
source: We found that controls' P2 recovery was significantly slower than dyslexics'.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2b.

claim: The only significant difference between the two groups in passive P2 adaptation was in τ.
source: Importantly, the only significant difference between the two groups was in τ (τ for controls = 5.4 ± 0.8 s, τ for dyslexics = 3.3 ± 0.7 s; mean ± SEM; z = 3.3, p<0.005. Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The other two parameters (α and β) of passive P2 adaptation did not differ between the two groups.
source: The other two parameters did not differ between the two groups (α for controls = 490 ± 73 μV x ms, α for dyslexics = 410 ± 44 μV x ms; z = −0.04, n.s.; β for controls = −750 ± 112 μV x ms, β for dyslexics = −724 ± 100 μV x ms; z = −0.1, n.s. Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2b.

claim: In both groups, P2 responses were the smallest in the block with the shortest ISI (2 s) in the passive condition.
source: In both groups, P2 responses were the smallest in the block with the shortest ISI (2 s), when P2 adaptation was still substantial, and increased (recovered) with longer ISIs, as adaptation gradually decayed (χ2 = 60.3, p<10−12. Friedman test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2b.

claim: Among dyslexics, P2 reached its peak magnitude by 6.5 s ISI in the passive condition.
source: Among dyslexics, P2 reached its peak magnitude by 6.5 s ISI (Figure 4A, red dot-dashed line)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Controls' P2 was larger at 9.5 s than at 6.5 s ISIs in the passive condition.
source: whereas controls' P2 was larger at 9.5 s than at 6.5 s ISIs (Figure 4A, blue dotted line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Among controls, the estimated duration of P2 adaptation was longer in the active than in the passive condition.
source: Interestingly, among controls, the estimated duration of P2 adaptation was longer in the active than in the passive condition (P2: z = 3, p<0.005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: The prolongation of P2 adaptation by behavioral context was not observed in the dyslexic group.
source: This was not observed in the dyslexic group (P2: z = 0.5, n.s. Wilcoxon tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: The interaction between group and condition (passive/active) in the estimated time constant of P2 adaptation was only marginally significant.
source: The interaction (in the estimated time constant of adaptation) between group and condition (passive/active) was only marginally significant (z = 1.8, p=0.07 Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: Controls' but not dyslexics' P2 adaptation was prolonged by introducing a behavioral context.
source: Thus, controls' but not dyslexics' P2 adaptation was prolonged by introducing a behavioral context.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data comparing active and passive conditions.

claim: A consistent group difference was found under both passive and active conditions in the dynamics of P2 adaptation.
source: Overall, we found a consistent group difference under both passive and active conditions in the dynamics of P2 adaptation, in line with our a priori hypothesis (based on Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015) regarding P2.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: A significant group difference in the dynamics of N1 was found when listeners were actively performing the task.
source: We also found a significant group difference in the dynamics of N1 when listeners were actively performing the task.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2a.

claim: A significant group difference under passive conditions was found only for P2.
source: But, a significant group difference under passive conditions was found only for P2.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2b.

claim: Participants' response times were shorter in the second presentation of the same non-word.
source: Participants' response times (RTs, measured as vocal response onset) were shorter in the second presentation of the same non-word.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The magnitude of improvement in reading RTs declined as the time interval from the previous presentation of the same non-word increased.
source: However, the magnitude of this improvement declined as the time interval from the previous presentation of the same non-word increased (i.e. when there were more intervening words).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics' RTs were longer than controls' in the reading task.
source: Overall, dyslexics' RTs were longer than controls' (controls — n = 29; mean RT per word ± SEM = 725 ± 28 ms; dyslexics — n = 23; mean RT ± SEM = 929 ± 47 ms; z = 3.3, p<0.001. Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics were less accurate than controls in the reading task.
source: and they were less accurate (controls — mean % correct ± SEM = 98.6 ± 0.3; dyslexics — 96.0 ± 1.4; z = 3.2, p<0.005. Mann-Whitney U test), as expected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Both groups showed large recent context (repetition) effects in reading.
source: Both groups showed large recent context (repetition) effects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Both groups showed substantially faster reading RTs in the second than in the first encounter with the same non-word when the words were proximal in time (<2 s interval).
source: Specifically, both groups showed substantially faster reading RTs in the second than in the first encounter with the same non-word, when the words were proximal in time (<2 s interval), even though they were never consecutive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics' benefit from repetition was similar to controls' when the second presentation occurred within <2 s ITI.
source: In these trials, dyslexics' benefit from repetition was similar to controls' (Figure 5B; mean benefit ± SEM for controls — 25% ± 2% or 170 ± 19 ms, for dyslexics — 23% ± 3% or 177 ± 20 ms; z = 0.1, n.s. Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In trials with larger inter-word intervals, dyslexics' benefits from repetition were smaller than controls'.
source: However, in trials with larger inter-word intervals, dyslexics' benefits were smaller. Importantly, dyslexics' benefits were smaller than controls', even though their starting point had longer RTs, as explained above (mean ITI of 42 s, max. ITI of 163 s; mean benefit ± SEM for controls — 12% ± 1% or 90 ± 10 ms, for dyslexics — 6% ± 1% or 52 ± 8 ms, z = 3, p<0.005. Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Among dyslexics, the difference in benefit from repetitions with small (<2 s) compared to larger (>2 s) intervals was greater than this difference among controls.
source: Indeed, among dyslexics, the difference in benefit from repetitions with small (<2 s) compared to larger (>2 s) intervals was greater than this difference among controls (z = 2.2, p<0.05; Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics' faster decay is consistent with a time-based effect rather than with an enhanced interference effect.
source: Thus, here too, dyslexics' faster decay is consistent with a time-based effect rather than with an enhanced interference effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Dyslexics' behavioral benefits declined faster both in the context of reading and in sound discrimination.
source: We characterized the dynamics of context effects, and found that they differ consistently between dyslexics and good readers. Dyslexics' behavioral benefits declined faster, both in the context of reading and in sound discrimination.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiments 2a and 3.

claim: In both groups, the behavioral dynamics reflected the dynamics of cortical adaptation.
source: In both groups, the behavioral dynamics reflected the dynamics of cortical adaptation, which decayed faster in dyslexics, both when actively performing a task and in passive listening.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: Cortical adaptation decayed faster in dyslexics both when actively performing a task and in passive listening.
source: In both groups, the behavioral dynamics reflected the dynamics of cortical adaptation, which decayed faster in dyslexics, both when actively performing a task and in passive listening.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: Dyslexics' shorter time constant of adaptation reflects a shorter time constant of implicit sound integration.
source: We propose that dyslexics' shorter time constant of adaptation reflects a shorter time constant of implicit sound integration.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Dyslexics' faster decay decreases the time constant of their integration of sound statistics.
source: Dyslexics' faster decay decreases the time constant of their integration of sound statistics, and consequently reduces the reliability of their implicitly calculated priors.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Dyslexics' faster decay reduces the reliability of their implicitly calculated priors.
source: Dyslexics' faster decay decreases the time constant of their integration of sound statistics, and consequently reduces the reliability of their implicitly calculated priors.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Owing to noisier priors, attaining the same level of processing reliability requires the extraction of more on-line information.
source: Owing to their noisier priors, attaining the same level of processing reliability requires the extraction of more on-line information, which requires more processing time, leading to the stereotypic 'slower processing time' in dyslexia.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on inference from the findings.

claim: Extracting more on-line information requires more processing time, leading to the stereotypic 'slower processing time' in dyslexia.
source: Owing to their noisier priors, attaining the same level of processing reliability requires the extraction of more on-line information, which requires more processing time, leading to the stereotypic 'slower processing time' in dyslexia.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on inference from the findings.

claim: This account explains dyslexics' often poorer performance on rapidly presented brief auditory stimuli for both simple tones and speech.
source: This account explains dyslexics' often poorer performance on rapidly presented brief auditory stimuli for both simple tones (Tallal, 1980; Temple et al., 2000) and speech (McArthur and Bishop, 2005; Boets et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative claim that the proposed account explains previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Dyslexics' poor short term memory skills are amply documented.
source: On the one hand, dyslexics' poor short term memory skills are amply documented (Beneventi et al., 2010; Banai and Yifat, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dyslexics are known to perform poorly with short stimuli presented at brief intervals.
source: On the other hand, dyslexics are known to perform poorly with short stimuli presented at brief intervals (Tallal, 1980), suggesting that they should gain from longer inter-stimulus intervals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The seemingly contradictory observations about dyslexics' performance result from the same basic impairment.
source: We claim that these seemingly contradictory observations result from the same basic impairment.
evidence: This is a speculative claim that unifies previous observations.

claim: The more predictable the stimuli are for controls, the greater relative slowness dyslexics are expected to show.
source: The more predictable the stimuli are for controls, both locally within session and globally in terms of long-term regularities (such as in language) the greater relative slowness ('slow processing speed') dyslexics are expected to show (consistent with Ahissar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed account, consistent with previous research.

claim: Dyslexics only benefitted less from prior statistics in the case of longer-term effects (>2 s).
source: It served to dissociate the benefits of very short-term (<2 s; the scale attributed to working memory processes; Baddeley, 2010) implicit effects from somewhat longer-term effects. Dyslexics only benefitted less from prior statistics in the latter case.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Dyslexics' noisier priors may lead to slower long-term learning of characteristic sound regularities.
source: Dyslexics' noisier priors (predictions based on past experiences) may lead to slower long-term learning of characteristic sound regularities, such as those in the native language (Nicolson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about long-term consequences, with a citation to related research.

claim: Dyslexics should benefit less than controls from a given number of experiences.
source: It follows that dyslexics should benefit less than controls from a given number of experiences, and that group differences should increase with additional specific experiences.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed account.

claim: Group differences should increase with additional specific experiences.
source: It follows that dyslexics should benefit less than controls from a given number of experiences, and that group differences should increase with additional specific experiences.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed account.

claim: Although both good and poor readers are expected to improve with practice, dyslexics' benefits per exposure are expected to be smaller.
source: Thus, although both good and poor readers are expected to improve with practice, dyslexics' benefits per exposure are expected to be smaller.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed account.

claim: Counterintuitively, dyslexics' relative difficulties are expected to be greater for highly trained stimuli.
source: Hence, counterintuitively, dyslexics' relative difficulties are expected to be greater for highly trained stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed account.

claim: The observation of reduced repetition effects in dyslexics' reading rate is compatible with imaging observations by Pugh et al. (2008).
source: Our observation of reduced repetition effects in dyslexics' reading rate is compatible with imaging observations by Pugh et al. (2008), who compared the impact of word repetition in reading on BOLD activation in posterior reading-related areas, in dyslexics versus controls.
evidence: This claim relates the current findings to previous research.

claim: Pugh et al. (2008) found that although both populations gained from repetitions, the impact differed between groups.
source: They found that although both populations gained from such repetitions, the impact differed between groups.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited research.

claim: Controls' activation was monotonically reduced with repetitions in the Pugh et al. (2008) study.
source: Whereas controls' activation was monotonically reduced with repetitions, dyslexics' activation initially increased.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited research.

claim: Dyslexics' activation initially increased with repetitions in the Pugh et al. (2008) study.
source: Whereas controls' activation was monotonically reduced with repetitions, dyslexics' activation initially increased.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited research.

claim: Dyslexics' slower learning rate per event was also proposed by Nicolson et al. (2010).
source: Interestingly, dyslexics' slower learning rate per event (or exposure) was also proposed by Nicolson et al. (2010), who based their argument on slower learning curves in a different context.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nicolson et al. (2010) found that dyslexics exhibit slower learning of simple motor tasks.
source: They found that dyslexics exhibit slower learning of simple motor tasks, which perhaps tap mechanisms that are partially common to those used in serial comparison tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited research.

claim: Dyslexics' P2 component had a shorter adaptation duration under both active and passive conditions.
source: We found that dyslexics' P2 component had a shorter adaptation duration under both active and passive conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiments 2a and 2b.

claim: Dyslexics' N1 had a shorter adaptation duration under the active condition when compared to controls.
source: We also found that their N1 had a shorter adaptation duration under the active condition when compared to controls.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2a.

claim: The P2 component reflects the accumulation of sound statistics automatically, without explicit attention.
source: The P2 (which peaks 200 ms after tone onset) component was shown to reflect the accumulation of sound statistics (Tremblay et al., 2010; Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015) automatically, without explicit attention (Sheehan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: P2 was shown to be abnormal among dyslexics.
source: Moreover, it was shown to be abnormal among dyslexics (Bishop and McArthur, 2004; Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dynamics of P2 matched those of the behavioral context effects measured simultaneously.
source: Indeed, its dynamics matched those of the behavioral context effects measured simultaneously.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2a.

claim: The earlier N1 component had a shorter time constant among dyslexics under the active condition.
source: However, even the earlier N1 component (100 ms) had a shorter time constant here among dyslexics under the active condition.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2a.

claim: Whether N1 and P2 originate from one or two cortical generators is still unclear.
source: Whether these two components originate from one or two cortical generators is still unclear (e.g. Mayhew et al., 2010; Lanting et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies have found that the magnitudes of adaptation of both N1 and P2 are sensitive to the statistics that characterize the experiment.
source: Nevertheless, recent studies have found that the magnitudes of adaptation of both are sensitive to the statistics that characterize the experiment (e.g. Herrmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A shorter time constant of adaptation was found in N1 than in P2.
source: We found a shorter time constant of adaptation in N1 than in P2.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Experiment 2a.

claim: The observations suggest that the dynamics of adaptation in the auditory cortex of dyslexics differs from that of controls.
source: Our observations suggest that the dynamics of adaptation in the auditory cortex of dyslexics differs from that of controls.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The observations do not directly point to the anatomical source of the abnormality.
source: But they do not directly point to the anatomical source of this abnormality as 100–200 ms ERP signals reflect the combined contribution of various brain sites.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's methodology.

claim: Dyslexics' processing deficit is likely to result from a structural variation which probably has a genetic origin.
source: Thus, although dyslexics' processing deficit is likely to result from a structural variation (which probably has a genetic origin; Giraud and Ramus, 2013), our observations are consistent with several accounts.
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The abnormally fast decay of N1 and P2 adaptation may reflect a different anatomy of the auditory cortex.
source: The abnormally fast decay of N1 and P2 adaptation may reflect a different anatomy of the auditory cortex, as suggested in a recent longitudinal study (Clark et al., 2014), or impaired long-range connectivity between posterior and frontal areas (Boets et al., 2013; Ramus, 2014), which are not mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The abnormally fast decay of N1 and P2 adaptation may reflect impaired long-range connectivity between posterior and frontal areas.
source: The abnormally fast decay of N1 and P2 adaptation may reflect a different anatomy of the auditory cortex, as suggested in a recent longitudinal study (Clark et al., 2014), or impaired long-range connectivity between posterior and frontal areas (Boets et al., 2013; Ramus, 2014), which are not mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several accounts of dyslexics' auditory processing deficits are consistent with the current findings, including impaired top-down control.
source: With respect to nature of dyslexics' auditory processing deficits, several accounts are consistent with our current findings. These include both impaired top-down control (Díaz et al., 2012), and unreliable (i.e. more variable) auditory responses (Hornickel and Kraus, 2013) associated with seemingly noisier sensory systems (Sperling et al., 2005), particularly in some frequency bands (Goswami et al., 2002; Goswami, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative claim that various accounts are consistent with the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Several accounts of dyslexics' auditory processing deficits are consistent with the current findings, including unreliable auditory responses.
source: With respect to nature of dyslexics' auditory processing deficits, several accounts are consistent with our current findings. These include both impaired top-down control (Díaz et al., 2012), and unreliable (i.e. more variable) auditory responses (Hornickel and Kraus, 2013) associated with seemingly noisier sensory systems (Sperling et al., 2005), particularly in some frequency bands (Goswami et al., 2002; Goswami, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative claim that various accounts are consistent with the findings, supported by citations.

claim: All these observations are expected outcomes of poorer implicit predictions made on the basis of stimuli statistics.
source: All these observations are expected outcomes of poorer implicit predictions made on the basis of stimuli statistics.
evidence: This is a speculative claim that unifies various observations.

claim: When dyslexics' behavioral sensitivity to complex and challenging noise stimuli was assessed, their impairment is specific for repeated stimuli (with >2 sec intervals).
source: Indeed, when dyslexics' behavioral sensitivity to complex and challenging noise stimuli was assessed, it was found that their impairment is specific for repeated stimuli (with >2 sec intervals).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Daikhin et al., 2016).

claim: Dyslexics' performance tended to be even better than controls' when stimuli differed from the repeated, and hence implicitly predicted, ones.
source: Moreover, their performance tended to be even better than controls' when stimuli differed from the repeated, and hence implicitly predicted, ones (Daikhin et al., 2016; for visual analog see also Jaffe-Dax et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The involvement of the auditory cortex does not exclude the contribution of sub-cortical regions.
source: Importantly, the involvement of the auditory cortex does not exclude the contribution of sub-cortical regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Both the cerebellum and the basal ganglia are involved in the process of integrating sound regularities into improved perceptual performance.
source: Both the cerebellum and the basal ganglia are involved in the process of integrating sound regularities into improved perceptual performance with reduced reliance on on-line working memory processes and increased reliance on specific sound predictions (Daikhin and Ahissar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The hypothesis linking dyslexics' reduced rate of automatization with impaired usage of cerebellar processes is in line with the current findings and interpretation.
source: Thus, the hypothesis linking dyslexics' reduced rate of automatization (in reading and in other tasks) with impaired usage of cerebellar processes (Nicolson and Fawcett, 1990; Nicolson et al., 2010) is also in line with our findings and interpretation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim that the current findings are consistent with previous hypotheses, supported by citations.

claim: There may not be a single anatomical source of difficulty in dyslexia.
source: The attempts to map dyslexics' processing difficulties to several potentially relevant anatomical abnormalities suggest that there may not be a single anatomical source of difficulty, and that the issue of the core deficit underlying dyslexia should be seen as process-related rather than structure-related.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings and previous research.

claim: The issue of the core deficit underlying dyslexia should be seen as process-related rather than structure-related.
source: The attempts to map dyslexics' processing difficulties to several potentially relevant anatomical abnormalities suggest that there may not be a single anatomical source of difficulty, and that the issue of the core deficit underlying dyslexia should be seen as process-related rather than structure-related.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings and previous research.

claim: The observation that the process of dyslexics' neural adaptation is abnormally short paves the way for future studies of the neural processes that underlie reading difficulties in non-humans.
source: Our observation that the process of dyslexics' neural adaptation is abnormally short paves the way for future studies of the neural processes that underlie reading difficulties in non-humans.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: Adaptation reflects a mechanism for statistical learning.
source: An important insight suggested by our study, which is further supported by recent human studies in speech perception (e.g. Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2016), is that adaptation reflects a mechanism for statistical learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: This interpretation is in line with recent animal studies suggesting that adaptation reflects a mechanism for making implicit high-resolution stimulus predictions.
source: This interpretation is in line with recent animal studies, suggesting that adaptation reflects a mechanism for making implicit high-resolution stimulus predictions on the basis of an experiment's statistics (Khouri and Nelken, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neural adaptation occurs at multiple time scales, as observed both in animals and in humans.
source: Another studied aspect of neural adaptation is its occurrence at multiple time scales, as observed both in animals (Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Khouri and Nelken, 2015) and in humans (reviewed in Lu and Sperling, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dyslexics' deficit is characterized at time scales >2 s after stimulus presentation.
source: Here we propose that dyslexics' deficit is characterized at time scales >2 s after stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: About half of the dyslexic participants showed adaptation time scales that were within the range of controls.
source: About half of our dyslexic participants showed adaptation time scales that were within the range of controls (Figures 2–4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The partial overlap between the two groups could have stemmed from the low reliability of the measurements.
source: This partial overlap between the two groups could have stemmed from the low reliability of our measurements.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability.

claim: Another potential source for the variability might be different types of dyslexia among the dyslexic participants.
source: Another potential source for this variability might be different types of dyslexia among our dyslexic participants, which may relate to different underlying neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability.

claim: The standard reading tests used for inclusion or exclusion of participants might not have been fine-grained enough to define participants along dimensions that map to different sources of underlying difficulties.
source: The standard reading tests that were used for inclusion or exclusion of participants might not have been fine-grained enough to define participants along the dimensions that map to different sources of underlying difficulties (Zoccolotti and Friedmann, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability, with a citation to related research.

claim: The Bayesian framework with the principle of efficient coding predicts that more likely stimuli gradually acquire denser, more reliable representations.
source: One putative conceptual link may be provided by the Bayesian framework, when the principle of efficient coding is introduced (Wei et al., 2015). This principle predicts that more likely stimuli gradually acquire denser, more reliable representations.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on a theoretical framework, supported by a citation.

claim: The typical gradual enhancement of the representation of more likely stimuli may be reduced in dyslexia.
source: The typical gradual enhancement of the representation of more likely stimuli may be reduced in dyslexia, leading to reduced sensitivity to the specific phonological and morphological forms that characterize native language.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the long-term consequences of the observed deficit.

claim: Reduced enhancement of representations may lead to reduced sensitivity to the specific phonological and morphological forms that characterize native language.
source: The typical gradual enhancement of the representation of more likely stimuli may be reduced in dyslexia, leading to reduced sensitivity to the specific phonological and morphological forms that characterize native language.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the long-term consequences of the observed deficit.

claim: Sixty native Hebrew speakers (30 dyslexics and 30 good readers) were recruited for the study.
source: Sixty native Hebrew speakers (30 dyslexics and 30 good readers), all of whom were students at the Hebrew University [mean age (STD) = 24.2 (5.4) years; 36 females] were recruited for this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All dyslexic participants had been diagnosed as having a specific reading disability by authorized clinicians.
source: All dyslexic participants had been diagnosed as having a specific reading disability by authorized clinicians.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for dyslexic participants.

claim: Participants with more than 2 years of formal musical education were excluded.
source: Participants with more than 2 years of formal musical education were excluded, so that musical training would not be a major contributor to their pitch sensitivity (Micheyl et al., 2006; Parbery-Clark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria, with citations explaining the rationale.

claim: Participants with poor Block Design scores (lower than a normalized score of 7) were excluded from the study.
source: Participants with poor Block Design scores (lower than a normalized score of 7) were also excluded from the study.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria.

claim: Dyslexics differed from controls in all phonological tasks and in verbal working memory, but not in their general reasoning skills.
source: Dyslexics differed from their good-reader peers in all phonological tasks and in verbal working memory, but not in their general reasoning skills (Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is supported by the cognitive assessment data presented in Table 1.
